title: French Onion Soup
subtitle: Deeply caramelised onion broth with a Gruyere crouton
excerpt: Onions cooked very slowly until deeply caramelised and sweet, simmered in beef stock and white wine, then finished with a toasted baguette crouton and a thick cap of melted Gruyere. Classic and unhurried.

recipe.sourceNotes: French onion soup (soupe a l'oignon) is one of France's most celebrated soups, with roots in Parisian working-class cuisine. It was a staple of the Les Halles market workers, who ate it at all hours in the surrounding restaurants. The modern restaurant version, with gratineed croutons and Gruyere, was standardised in the mid-20th century. The key technique is time: the onions must be cooked very slowly for at least 45 minutes to develop deep colour and sweetness. Rushing the caramelisation is the most common mistake.

content.text: The caramelisation takes a minimum of 45 minutes over very low heat: do not try to speed it up with higher heat. The onions will first soften and turn translucent, then golden, then deep amber. At each stage the colour should deepen slowly. If the bottom of the pan starts to stick, add a splash of water and scrape up the residue: this is flavour.

Melt the butter and oil together in a large, heavy-based saucepan over very low heat. Add all the sliced onions. Stir to coat. Cook uncovered for 45 to 50 minutes, stirring every 5 to 10 minutes, until the onions are deep golden brown and very soft. Add the garlic in the last 10 minutes.

Add the white wine. Turn up the heat and cook for 3 minutes, scraping up any sticky residue from the bottom. Add the stock, thyme, and bay leaves. Simmer for 20 minutes. Season with salt and pepper. Remove the thyme and bay leaves.

Toast the baguette slices. Ladle the soup into oven-proof bowls. Place 2 croutons on top of each bowl. Cover with a generous layer of Gruyere. Place under a hot grill for 3 to 4 minutes until the cheese is melted and bubbling. Serve immediately.
